summary: Specifies the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) data plane for MPLS networks. It reuses existing pseudowire encapsulations and MPLS Traffic Engineering mechanisms, building on the DetNet architecture and data plane framework to carry time-sensitive flows.

eli5.summary: A way to run guaranteed on-time delivery lanes over label-switched networks by reusing tools those networks already have.

subtitle: How Deterministic Networking flows are carried over MPLS using pseudowire-style labels and a control word with sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) needs very low packet loss and bounded delivery latency, which requires flows to be identified, sequenced, replicated and given reserved resources across an MPLS network.
tldr.mechanism: A DetNet packet carries a DetNet Control Word with a sequence number, an S-Label that identifies the service, and zero or more F-Labels that steer it along a traffic-engineered LSP. Existing pseudowire and MPLS-TE mechanisms are reused.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that defines the on-wire encapsulation and node behavior; label distribution, resource control and OAM details are left to the controller plane and other documents.

today: RFC 8964 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the DetNet architecture in RFC 8655 and the data plane framework in RFC 8938.

sections.title: DetNet over MPLS
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is a service a network can offer to DetNet flows. It provides delivery with extremely low packet loss rates and bounded end-to-end delivery latency. General concepts are in the DetNet architecture, RFC 8655.

The architecture splits DetNet data plane functions into two sub-layers. The service sub-layer provides service functions such as protection and reordering, using the Packet Replication, Elimination and Ordering Functions (PREOF). The forwarding sub-layer provides forwarding assurance: low loss, assured latency and limited out-of-order delivery.

This RFC specifies the data plane operation and on-wire encapsulation of DetNet flows over an MPLS packet switched network. How MPLS-encapsulated DetNet is carried over different underlying network technologies, and the types of traffic carried, are out of scope. Background common to all DetNet data planes is in RFC 8938.
sections.eli5: Some data, like control signals for a factory machine, must arrive on time and almost never get lost. This document shows how to give such data a special delivery lane on label-switched networks.

sections.title: Sub-Layers, Labels and Node Types
sections.content:
The design reuses pseudowire (PW) encapsulations and MPLS Traffic Engineering. The RFC introduces these terms:

  • S-Label: a service label used between nodes that implement the service sub-layer. It identifies a DetNet flow at the receiving node.
  • F-Label: a forwarding label that identifies the LSP used to forward a flow, a hop-by-hop label between Label Switching Routers.
  • A-Label: a special case of an S-Label used for aggregation, whose properties are known only at the aggregation and deaggregation end points.
  • d-CW: the DetNet Control Word, which carries sequencing information.

In the label stack the service sub-layer sits at the bottom (d-CW and S-Label) and the F-Labels are on top. Three node roles appear. End systems and relay nodes understand DetNet and perform service and forwarding sub-layer functions, behaving like T-PEs at the edge of an MPLS domain and S-PEs in the middle. Transit nodes may be DetNet-aware or ordinary LSRs that still provide the traffic engineering and QoS needed to meet the flows' requirements. The control and management planes may use RSVP-TE, MPLS-TP or MPLS Segment Routing extended for resource allocation.
sections.eli5: Each packet wears two kinds of labels. The inside one says which reserved lane it belongs to, and the outside ones say which road to take next.

sections.title: The Encapsulation and the DetNet Control Word
sections.content:
The encapsulation has a d-CW, an S-Label, zero or more F-Labels, and then the usual data-link encapsulation. With penultimate hop popping, there may be no F-Label on the final hop.

The d-CW follows the Generic PW MPLS Control Word of RFC 4385 and MUST be present in every DetNet packet that contains application flow data. Bits 0 to 3 are zero and bits 4 to 31 hold an unsigned sequence number. The sequence number space is circular with no restriction on the initial value.

Nodes MUST support three sequence number lengths: 0, 16 and 28 bits, provisioned per DetNet service. With 0 bits the field is all zeros on every packet. With 16 or 28 bits the number is incremented by one for each new packet, and with 16 bits, d-CW bits 4 to 15 are set to zero. Values can wrap, and zero is an ordinary sequence number, which differs from RFC 4448, where zero means the check is not used. The 16-bit length supports some legacy clients, and the 28-bit length avoids wrap while packets are in flight in high-speed networks.
sections.eli5: The control word is a ticket number stapled to each packet. The receiver uses the numbers to spot duplicates and to put packets back in order.

sections.title: S-Labels, F-Labels and PREOF
sections.content:
Edge and end-system nodes MUST push and pop the d-CW and S-Label, and relay nodes MAY swap S-Label values. S-Labels are allocated by the receiving side, may come from the platform label space, and MUST be provisioned per service by the controller plane. When the platform label space is not used, the preceding F-Labels (and possibly the incoming interface) must be used together with the S-Label to identify the service.

Three functions make up PREOF:

  • Packet Replication Function (PRF): sends the same application data over multiple member flows on separate LSPs, with an S-Label configured per member flow and the same d-CW value on every copy.
  • Packet Elimination Function (PEF): discards duplicate instances of a sequence number. It MUST NOT be used with a 0-bit sequence number field.
  • Packet Ordering Function (POF): processes packets in the order given by the sequence number. The number of out-of-order packets handled also affects flow latency.

All three are optional (MAY) and each is turned on by configuration. A relay node MUST preserve the sequence number through elimination and replication. Network changes to an LSP carrying DetNet MUST be loop-free, because a replicating node that received its own copies would make a loop more destructive than a unicast loop.

F-Labels give the forwarding sub-layer explicit routes and allocated resources, using ordinary push, pop and swap. A node MAY be an unmodified MPLS LSR if existing TE mechanisms meet the flow's needs. Nodes MUST discard or remark packets not tied to a completed resource allocation, MUST NOT let such packets use DetNet-allocated resources, and MUST keep QoS and CoS flows within their allocations.
sections.eli5: Sending two copies down different tracks protects against a lost copy. The receiver keeps the first copy of each numbered packet, throws away the second, and can sort them by number.

sections.title: OAM, Aggregation and Service Classes
sections.content:
OAM follows RFC 5085, with the restriction that only VCCV type 1 is supported. When the first nibble of the d-CW is 0x0 the payload is user data, and when it is 0x1 the payload is OAM. Further DetNet OAM considerations are left for further study.

Aggregation can be done with hierarchical LSPs (RFC 4206) or by layering DetNet flows under an A-Label, where each flow keeps its own d-CW and S-Label so PREOF still works. Resource control for aggregates belongs to the controller plane.

For Class of Service, the existing MPLS Diffserv architecture (RFC 3270) is used, and both E-LSP and L-LSP modes MAY be used. MPLS ECN MAY also be used. For Quality of Service, a baseline comes from MPLS-TE (RFC 3209, RFC 3473) and can be combined with the underlying network layer such as IEEE 802.1 TSN. Service definitions are cited from RFC 2211, RFC 2212 and RFC 6003, and more are expected in future documents.
sections.eli5: The first digit of the control word tells whether a packet is real cargo or a check-up message. Several small shipments can also ride inside one big labeled container.

sections.title: Control Information and Security
sections.content:
Section 5 lists what a controller must provision: for the service sub-layer, the sequence number length (0, 16 or 28 bits), the outgoing and incoming S-Labels, whether PRF, PEF or POF is used, and the link to forwarding sub-layer information. For the forwarding sub-layer it lists the F-Label stack, traffic parameters, interfaces and next hops. How labels are distributed (for example by RSVP-TE, NETCONF and YANG, BGP or PCEP) is out of scope.

On security, the RFC points to DetNet security work and RFC 8655, and notes that the considerations for MPLS networks in RFC 5920 apply. It does not add or change any application header information. MPLS has no native confidentiality or integrity services, so application flows rely on mechanisms such as IPsec or MACsec. Per-flow identification can give controller-plane attackers more information. Against DoS and delay attacks, it suggests policing and shaping, ensuring only intended devices are on an LSP, and monitoring LSP delay, with traffic moved to another path if a delay attack is suspected. IANA has no actions.
sections.eli5: A controller must tell every stop on the route which labels and numbers to use. Because the network promises on-time delivery, it must also guard against anyone slowing packets down or flooding the lane.
